text: NVIDIA NIM packages optimized AI inference microservices as Docker containers that expose an OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 8000.
A NIM container bundles the model weights, an inference engine (TensorRT-LLM or vLLM), and a REST API layer so you can deploy an LLM with a single docker run command.
Because every NIM speaks the OpenAI chat completions schema, applications written against the OpenAI SDK can switch to a self-hosted NIM by changing only the base_url.
NVIDIA hosts a free tier of NIMs at integrate.api.nvidia.com so developers can prototype against the same models they will later self-host on their own GPUs.
The NIM Operator is a Kubernetes operator that installs and manages NIM microservices on a GPU cluster using Helm charts, handling model caching, autoscaling, and rolling upgrades.
TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's inference engine that compiles a trained large language model into a GPU-specific optimized engine using fused kernels, paged KV-cache, and FlashAttention-style attention.
TensorRT-LLM supports continuous batching and in-flight batching, which lets the server pack many concurrent requests into a single GPU forward pass for higher throughput.
A NIM auto-selects the correct TensorRT-LLM engine profile for the detected GPU on first launch, then caches the built engine under ~/.cache/nim so subsequent starts are fast.
Quantization such as FP8 or INT4 AWQ shrinks the model in VRAM and increases throughput, at the cost of a small quality drop; NIM ships quantized profiles for many models.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds an LLM's answer in an external corpus by retrieving relevant passages at query time and inserting them into the model's prompt as context.
An embedding model converts text into a fixed-length dense vector so that semantic similarity between two pieces of text becomes cosine similarity between their vectors.
A vector database stores embeddings and returns the top-k nearest neighbors to a query vector, typically using an approximate nearest-neighbor index like HNSW or IVF for scale.

A reranker is a cross-encoder that scores every (query, passage) pair jointly and reorders the top-k candidates from the retriever; it is more accurate than embedding similarity but too slow to run over an entire corpus.

The standard RAG evaluation metrics are recall@k, which measures whether a relevant passage appears in the top-k, and mean reciprocal rank, which rewards putting the relevant passage higher in the list.
Chunking splits long documents into passages of a few hundred tokens each so that retrieval returns focused context; overlapping chunks help preserve information across chunk boundaries.
Every NIM exposes a Prometheus /metrics endpoint reporting request latency, tokens per second, GPU utilization, and queue depth, so it plugs straight into Grafana dashboards.
NIM exposes /v1/health/ready and /v1/health/live endpoints suitable for Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes, returning 200 only after the model engine is fully loaded.
You can scale a NIM horizontally by running multiple replicas behind a load balancer; the NIM Operator on Kubernetes automates this with a horizontal pod autoscaler tied to GPU utilization.
vLLM is an open-source LLM inference engine known for PagedAttention; NIM can use vLLM as a backend, but for supported models TensorRT-LLM usually delivers higher throughput on NVIDIA GPUs.

Triton Inference Server is a general-purpose model server that supports many backends including TensorRT-LLM, ONNX Runtime, and PyTorch; a NIM is essentially a preconfigured Triton plus model plus REST layer.
